metric_rationale: This metric isolates Trial 3 (A=[1, 0, 0, 1], B=[0, 1, 1, 1]), which is the only trial where Take The Best and Tallying make strictly opposite predictions. Take The Best predicts the subject will choose the option with a 1 on the most valid cue (feature 0), which is [1, 0, 0, 1]. Conversely, Tallying predicts the subject will choose the option with more positive features, which is [0, 1, 1, 1] (3 features vs 2). The metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the Take The Best-favored option on this specific trial pair. TTB will yield a value close to 1, while Tallying will yield a value close to 0, ensuring maximum discrimination.

In the experimental design, Trials 8 and 11 represent critical cases where Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) fundamentally diverge in their confidence. For Trial 8, Option A wins on feature 3 while Option B wins on feature 0. Tallying sees a 1-1 tie and guesses (50% choice probability). TTB, however, uses the highest validity feature (feature 0) and deterministically chooses B. For Trial 11, Option A wins on feature 1 and Option B wins on feature 2. Tallying again sees a 1-1 tie and guesses, while TTB looks at the first discriminating feature (feature 1) and deterministically chooses A. This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with TTB's definitive predictions on these two specific trials. TTB will score close to 2.0 (minus lapse noise), whereas Tallying will score around 1.0 because it guesses randomly on both.

Under the Tallying heuristic, the number of strictly winning features for the favored option is exactly 1 (and 0 for the other) across all four of these trials. Thus, Tallying predicts identical choice probabilities for the better option in all four trials, making the difference metric zero in expectation. Under the Advocated WADD theory (using a ratio-based Luce choice rule), the magnitude of the weighted sum heavily impacts choice probabilities. Trials 4 and 8 have a much larger ratio of evidence (~2.4) compared to Trials 1 and 12 (~1.3), so WADD predicts a significantly higher accuracy on the former pair, making the metric strongly positive.

Under Tallying, all features are weighted equally. In Trial 9 (A=[1, 1, 0, 0], B=[0, 0, 0, 1]) and Trial 10 (A=[0, 0, 1, 1], B=[0, 1, 0, 0]), Option A wins on exactly 2 features and Option B wins on exactly 1 feature. Thus, Tallying predicts the exact same probability of choosing A for both trials. Under WADD, the weighted sum for Trial 9 heavily favors A (1.89 vs 0.55, ratio=3.43) because A has the most valid features, whereas for Trial 10 the weighted sum favors A much less (1.21 vs 0.94, ratio=1.28). Thus, WADD predicts a much higher probability of choosing A on Trial 9 than on Trial 10. The metric measures the difference in the rate of choosing B (response=1) between Trial 10 and Trial 9, which equals P(Choose A)_9 - P(Choose A)_10. It will be near 0 for Tallying and strictly positive for WADD.

Focuses on two specific diagnostic trials (Trials 11 and 12) where Right-to-Left Take-The-Best (R2L-TTB) strongly contradicts Tallying. For example, in Trial 11, Option A has more positive features (wins 2-1 overall, favoring Tallying), but Option B has a positive feature at the rightmost index while Option A does not (favoring R2L-TTB). The metric calculates the proportion of choices across these trial types that align with R2L-TTB.

Focuses on trial 9 where Option A is [0, 1, 1, 0] and Option B is [0, 0, 0, 1]. Tallying prefers Option A because it wins on two features compared to Option B's one feature. R2L-TTB, processing from right to left, immediately selects Option B because it wins on the rightmost feature (index 3). The metric calculates the proportion of times the choice aligns with the R2L-TTB prediction (i.e., choosing the [0, 0, 0, 1] option), yielding ~0 for Tallying and ~1 for R2L-TTB.

This metric isolates trials where the two theories make strictly opposite predictions. It identifies the 'conflict trials' where the first discriminating cue from the left favors one option, but the first discriminating cue from the right favors the other. The metric calculates the proportion of choices on these conflict trials that align with the Right-to-Left TTB prediction. Under the R2L-TTB theory, this proportion will be close to 1 (minus noise), whereas under the standard TTB theory, it will be close to 0.

This metric isolates trials where the Left-to-Right (standard) Take-The-Best heuristic and the Right-to-Left TTB heuristic make strictly opposite predictions. It then calculates the proportion of decisions on these specific trials that align with the L2R prediction. Under the L2R theory, this value will be close to 1 (minus noise), while under the R2L theory, it will be close to 0 (plus noise). This creates a massive point estimate gap while maintaining low between-subject variance, easily passing the Welch's t-test.

In R2L-TTB, the choice probability depends solely on a fixed score difference (1 vs 0) for the winner, regardless of how many features favor it. Thus, R2L-TTB predicts that the probability of choosing B in Trial 1 (where B wins on all features) should be identical to the probability of choosing A in Trial 11 (where A wins on only the leftmost feature, and all other features are tied). In contrast, the Right-biased WADD model produces a massive score difference for Trial 1 (sum of all weights) but a very small score difference for Trial 11 (only the weight of the leftmost feature, gamma^0 = 1). Therefore, WADD predicts a much higher accuracy for Trial 1 than Trial 11, while R2L-TTB predicts a difference of zero.

The Competing Theory (Right-to-Left Take-The-Best) determines its choice based solely on the rightmost discriminating cue. It completely ignores all other cues, meaning its choice probability (driven by a constant softmax over [1,0]) is identical regardless of whether the remaining cues agree or disagree with the winner. The Advocated Theory (Right-biased Compensatory Model), however, integrates all cues. When the rightmost cue is opposed by other cues (Conflict trials), the net score difference between the options shrinks, reducing choice confidence compared to trials where all discriminating cues point in the same direction (Consistent trials). This metric calculates the difference in accuracy (relative to the R2L-TTB prediction) between Consistent and Conflict trials. The Competing Theory expects this difference to be exactly 0, while the Advocated Theory predicts a strictly positive difference.
